title: Creating bottom-up RNA transfer vehicles from synthetic protein assemblies.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed the Source Data workbook (761 KB XLSX, 12 sheets) and the 43-page Supplementary Information PDF. Counted the design-function screen directly: Fig 1f/g/h and Extended Data Fig 2 contain exactly 39 unique designed cage scaffolds (identifiers HE0482 ... HE0935) with 6 replicate values each for three readouts (release, uptake, messenger RNA delivery). Extended Data Fig 4f-h holds a second small screen of 22-24 membrane-binding domains named by UniProt accession or MGnify protein identifier. Supplementary Table 1 lists the same 39 scaffold names and about 91 long amino-acid sequences, but as a table inside a PDF. The article is Creative Commons Attribution 4.0, so everything downloads without login.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The abstract's claim of 'more than 100 bottom-up RNA transfer vehicles' (the Source Data only tabulates 39 scaffolds plus a few dozen domain variants); the in-vivo mouse and pig experiments; the claimed orders-of-magnitude advantage over lipid nanoparticles; and the existence of the RNA sequencing deposits (Sequence Read Archive PRJNA1489338, Gene Expression Omnibus GSE338002), which I confirmed resolve in NCBI but did not open.

a1_downloadable.note: Verified: Source Data XLSX (761 KB) and Supplementary Information PDF (10 MB) downloaded directly from Springer Nature with no login; article licence is Creative Commons Attribution 4.0.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Verified in the file: the three efficiency readouts are numeric values laid out as figure source data (constructs as columns, replicates as rows). It needs reshaping from wide to long, which is an hour of work, not construction by inference.

a3_inputs_present.note: Verified: amino-acid sequences for the scaffolds are present in Supplementary Table 1, but only inside a PDF table, so they would need PDF table extraction; membrane-binding domains are given as UniProt/MGnify accessions needing lookup (a few dozen, so tolerable).

a4_units_stated.note: Partly verified: values are fold-change luminescence ratios relative to a named control, with units explained in the figure legends and Supplementary Note 1, not inside the spreadsheet cells; absolute luminescence counts appear in some Extended Data sheets.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAILS. Counted in the file: 39 unique designed cage scaffolds with measured efficiency, plus a second screen of 22-24 membrane-binding domains. The modelling unit is the design, not the replicate well, so the largest honest training set is about 39-80 examples - far below the ~1,500 needed for regression and the ~400 for classification. The '>100 vehicles' in the abstract counts combinatorial assemblies, most of which have no tabulated screen value.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Observed before stopping: the whole dataset is one 761 KB workbook; trivially laptop-sized.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Observed: the paper says 'we screened 39 STV constructs' and the Source Data contains exactly 39 HE-coded scaffolds; Supplementary Table 1 lists the same 39 names.

a8_label_provenance.note: Observed: labels are physical luminescence measurements from a split-NanoLuciferase and split-firefly-luciferase reporter assay described in Supplementary Note 1 - a real measurement, not another model's output.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (a protein language model that turns an amino-acid sequence into a numeric vector)
backbone.hardware: CPU only; embedding 39-80 short sequences takes minutes

integration.partner_dataset: None pursued - evaluation stopped at the Part A sample-size killer.
integration.join_key: UniProt accession (present for the membrane-binding domains) and Protein Data Bank/design identifiers for the scaffolds
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Not written: with 39 measured designs there is no combination of this data with a large resource that could be evaluated honestly.

controls.positive_control: Would have been the paper's own reported finding that cyclic and dihedral symmetry scaffolds outperform icosahedral ones - a model must recover that ordering.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling, which with 39 examples would be indistinguishable from the real fit.
controls.external_validation: None found: no second laboratory has published the same split-luciferase release/uptake/delivery readout for designed protein cages.

honest_claim_h3: With 39 measured scaffolds, the only honest claim would be 'symmetry class and size correlate with delivery efficiency among the 39 designs this one laboratory chose to build', which is a descriptive statistic the paper already reports, not a predictive model.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a designed protein shell's sequence and symmetry to predict how well it carries messenger RNA into cells.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example would be one computer-designed protein cage: its amino-acid sequence, its symmetry type (icosahedral, dihedral or cyclic) and its subunit count. I verified only 39 such designs have measured efficiency values.
plain_idea.predict: Three numbers per design - how much particle is released from producer cells, how much is taken up by target cells, and how much cargo messenger RNA is functionally delivered - each measured as a luminescence fold-change in a split-luciferase reporter assay with six replicate wells.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Groups building protein-based gene-delivery vehicles (Helmholtz Munich, the Baker laboratory, several biotechs) currently pick scaffolds by trial and error, so a predictor would save months of cloning; but with 39 examples the result could not be trusted either way.

ml_idea: Predict release, cellular uptake and functional messenger RNA delivery efficiency of de-novo-designed protein cages from sequence and symmetry features, using a frozen protein language model plus a small regression head. Dead on sample size: 39 measured designs.

effort.compute_note: Estimated from the files I actually opened: a 761 KB workbook and ~91 sequences in a PDF table; embedding 39-80 short protein sequences with a small ESM-2 checkpoint on CPU is minutes. The 6 hours is mostly reshaping twelve figure-source-data blocks and extracting sequences from the PDF.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the distinct construct identifiers with a measured efficiency value in the Source Data workbook. I did this: 39 scaffolds (plus 22-24 membrane-binding domains), which kills the project in one command.

verdict_reason: A5 fails on verified counts. The Source Data workbook is fully open (Creative Commons Attribution 4.0), parses cleanly, and the labels are genuine luciferase measurements - but it contains only 39 unique designed cage scaffolds with measured release/uptake/delivery efficiency, plus a side screen of 22-24 membrane-binding domains. The abstract's '>100 vehicles' counts combinatorial assemblies that have no tabulated screen value. Six replicate wells per construct inflate the row count to a few hundred, but the modelling unit is the design, so this is the same 'A5 in disguise' failure as the scCT-DB candidate. No split, no held-out group and no honest confidence interval is possible at n=39; the symmetry-class effect the data supports is already reported in the paper as a figure.
